TEMPSENS INSTRUMENTS | CAPEX-LED SCALE-UP ACROSS THREE SEGMENTS

CAPEX — THE BIG GROWTH DRIVER
- Combined peak revenue potential exceeds ₹500 Cr.
- New capacities will commission in phases.
- Initial commissioning starts from Q4 FY27.
- Management sees potential revenue doubling by FY29–30.
- Around ₹500 Cr incremental revenue could come from capex.
- Potential FY29–30 revenue could approach ₹1,000 Cr.
- Potential EBITDA could reach ₹220–240 Cr.
- Potential PAT could reach ₹140–160 Cr.
- These estimates assume no margin expansion.

TEMPERATURE SENSING SOLUTIONS
- Q1 FY27 revenue grew 42% YoY.
- Brownfield expansion is currently underway.
- Commissioning is targeted for Q3 FY28.
- Peak incremental revenue potential is ₹120 Cr annually.
- Order pipeline remains healthy across multiple industries.
- Key sectors include nuclear, thermal, steel and glass.

TEMPERATURE SENSING — NEW PRODUCTS
- Non-contact temperature sensors are under development.
- Dispatches are expected from Q3 FY27.
- New products can expand the addressable market.
- Successful adoption could support future revenue diversification.

ELECTRICAL HEATING SOLUTIONS
- Q1 FY27 revenue increased 149% YoY.
- A new plant is being developed.
- Plant will manufacture MV heaters and custom furnaces.
- Commissioning is targeted for Q1 FY28.
- Peak revenue potential is approximately ₹200 Cr annually.
- This is currently the fastest-growing segment.

MEDIUM VOLTAGE HEATERS
- Medium Voltage Heaters are a new product opportunity.
- Applications include carbon capture and battery storage.
- Green hydrogen is another targeted application.
- Explosion-proof certification is targeted by Q4 FY27.
- Certification can unlock additional industrial applications.

SPECIALISED CABLES
- Q1 FY27 revenue declined 9% YoY.
- UL certification has now been obtained.
- Dispatches reached thermal industry customers.
- Oil & gas customers are also receiving supplies.
- Chemical customers have started receiving dispatches.
- Middle East oil-and-gas approvals remain underway.
- Approvals could open a new export market.

UNIT 8 — EXPORT EXPANSION
- A new export-focused Unit 8 is planned.
- Commissioning is targeted for Q2 FY28.
- Peak revenue potential is approximately ₹60 Cr annually.
- The facility should strengthen international cable opportunities.

TEMPSENS-VICTURA JV
- JV plant commissioning is targeted for Q4 FY27.
- Peak revenue potential is approximately ₹120 Cr annually.
- The JV adds another potential growth engine.
- Execution and customer ramp-up remain key monitorables.

NEW CABLE TECHNOLOGY
- High-temperature cable harnesses are under development.
- Target customers include OEMs.
- Successful qualification can create new applications.
- OEM relationships could provide recurring programme opportunities.

CAPEX-TO-REVENUE BRIDGE
- Current business provides the existing revenue base.
- New plants add significant manufacturing capacity.
- Capacity additions begin commissioning from Q4 FY27.
- Revenue contribution should increase through FY28.
- Full utilisation could support the FY29–30 targets.
- The core equation is:
  Capex → Capacity → Utilisation → Revenue → EBITDA → PAT

KEY CATALYSTS
- Temperature sensing expansion commissioning.
- Electrical heating plant commissioning.
- Medium Voltage Heater certification.
- Unit 8 commissioning.
- Tempsens-Victura JV commissioning.
- Non-contact sensor commercial dispatches.
- Middle East oil-and-gas approvals.
- High-temperature cable harness development.

WHAT TO WATCH
- Actual commissioning versus planned timelines.
- Incremental revenue from new facilities.
- Capacity utilisation after commissioning.
- Order-book growth across segments.
- MV heater certification progress.
- Middle East export approvals.
- JV plant customer additions.
- EBITDA and PAT conversion from incremental revenue.
- Working-capital requirements during rapid expansion.

KEY RISKS
- Capex commissioning could face delays.
- New capacity may ramp slower than expected.
- Revenue potential represents peak utilisation estimates.
- New products require customer acceptance.
- Export approvals could take longer.
- Working capital could increase during expansion.
- Actual margins may differ from management assumptions.

CRUX
- Tempsens is entering a significant capacity-led growth phase.
- Three segments provide multiple incremental growth opportunities.
- Electrical Heating is currently showing the strongest momentum.
- Temperature Sensing provides diversified industrial demand.
- Specialised Cables offer export and JV optionality.
- Management sees potential for approximately ₹1,000 Cr revenue.
- EBITDA could potentially reach ₹220–240 Cr.
- PAT could potentially reach ₹140–160 Cr.
- These targets depend heavily on execution.

KEY TAKEAWAY
- The story is shifting from organic growth to capacity-led scaling.
- Approximately ₹500 Cr incremental revenue potential is being created.
- Commissioning begins from Q4 FY27 across multiple projects.
- FY29–30 could therefore become the key monetisation period.
- The biggest monitorable is capex execution and utilisation.
- Concall commentary should provide greater visibility on demand.
- The next phase is converting capacity into revenue and earnings.

NO RECOMMENDATION
- Concall updates may provide further clarity today.
- Focus on capex, demand, commissioning and utilisation.
- Also track margins, working capital and order pipeline.

Final norms of MDR on UPI Payments, effective 15th Oct, 2026.

No impact on small-value UPI transactions up to ₹ 2,000, which comprise more than 95% of the total volume of UPI (P2M) transactions

A MDR of 0.4% will be introduced on Person-to-Merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹ 2,000/-. For transactions of ₹75,000/- and above, the MDR will be capped at ₹300 per transaction.

A dedicated fund will be established to subsidize and accelerate digital payment infrastructure in Tier 3 – 6 centres including NE states, J&K and Ladakh and in Tier 1 & 2 centres, any notified Scheme from Central Government shall also be included (such as PM SVANidhi, PM Vishwakarma etc.). Operational details to be out in 3m.

P2P transactions will continue to be free-of-cost for both payer as well as beneficiary. There will be no charges for any person transferring or receiving any amount to or from any other person (or even self-transfers) using UPI

UPI App providers shall NOT charge Platform Fee or any other charge for any payment made through UPI. UPI applications are explicitly restricted from levying platform fees on UPI transactions

There are no monthly quotas, volume limits, or tiered caps on free UPI transactions for individual consumers. Users can make as many valid person-to-person(P2P) or person-to-merchant (P2M) as necessary throughout the month without hitting a fee threshold.

Automated recurring standing instructions, known as UPI Mandates or AutoPay, do not carry prescribed MDR transaction charges.

Small merchants operating under the P2PM framework will continue with zero MDR. These are small vendors receiving up to Rs 1 lac per month through UPI QR directly into their accounts.

Existing QR infrastructure will continue to function normally. Merchants do not need to replace, re-register, or alter their existing physical QR stands or soundboxes.

For specific merchant categories such as railways, telecom services, insurance, and fuel, among others, a flat MDR of Rs 5 per transaction shall be applicable for transaction above Rs 2,000

The Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) for Capital Market transactions, including payments towards Mutual Funds, Securities, Stockbrokers, and Dealers, is set at a nominal 0.02% of the transaction value with a maximum capping of ₹300.

Insurance premium payments accepted via UPI qualify for specialised flat-rate concessions. For insurance premium payments exceeding ₹2,000, a flat MDR of ₹5 per transaction applies, rather than a percentage-based charge.

Fuel purchases made at petrol stations via UPI qualify for the flat concessional rate of ₹5 for payments over ₹2,000. For all fuel payments under ₹2,000, the MDR remains at 0%. 

Educational transactions up to ₹2,000 remain completely free of MDR.

Capacity Utilisation
Birla Tyres has roughly 400 tonnes/day installed capacity, but current production is only around 80–100 tonnes/day. That means utilisation is just ~20–25% of installed capacity.

Management wants to take utilisation to 100% over the next four years.

The company therefore doesn't initially need to build an entirely new manufacturing footprint to grow revenue dramatically.

Product mix

Historically, Birla Tyres had a meaningful presence in conventional truck & bus bias tyres.

Himadri is now deliberately shifting capacity toward:
=> OTR — Off-the-Road
=> OHT — Off-Highway
=> Agriculture tyres
=> Mining tyres
=> Construction/industrial tyres
=> Eventually PCR tyres
=> EV and SUV tyres

Around 400 new SKUs are planned to address specific customer requirements.

OTR/OHT - Profit engine

Agriculture and mining have been identified as the principal growth segments.

This is strategically attractive because specialised OTR/OHT tyres are more differentiated than commodity passenger or conventional CV tyres.

Himadri's FY26 annual report notes that agriculture and construction/mining/industrial tyre volumes had grown faster than several other tyre categories

So Birla Tyres is trying to position itself where:

Higher product differentiation + higher value/tyre + specialised applications = potentially better economics.

Export Strategy
Management wants >70% of OTR/OHT production to be exported.

Initial markets: Africa → West Asia → Europe → US

The company is simultaneously building an international distribution network.

Instead of competing primarily for domestic replacement-market share, Birla Tyres can tap global agriculture, mining and industrial demand.

EV tyres are the second leg of the story

OTR/OHT is the near-term focus but the longer-term opportunity is passenger-car radial tyres, particularly EVs, SUVs and specialised applications.

A dedicated PCR facility is targeted for FY28. This gives Birla Tyres another potential growth engine once the OTR/OHT ramp-up matures.

Things to track:
=> Execution
=> Capacity utilisation
=> Revenue/tonne
=> OTR/OHT share
=> Export contribution
=> EBITDA & cash generation

The most attractive part is that Himadri is trying to monetise an underutilised existing asset while simultaneously moving the product mix toward higher-value categories.

If utilisation rises meaningfully and OTR/OHT becomes the dominant mix, the operating leverage could be significant.

Birla trying to replicate Paint like disruption in Wire & Cables
India's W&C industry is a INR 1.1trn & growing at ~13% CAGR. Despite its size (0.3% of India GDP), industry remains fragmented with top 6 players control ~50% share

Market is roughly split into 3 equal buckets: Wires, LT Cables & MV/HT/EHV/Specialized Cables. Cables compared to wire is more organized, house wires have larger unorganized participation. Overall unorganized is > 30%

what attracted Birla. W&C sits at the intersection of electrification, urbanization & digitization. Housing, infra, renewables, data centres & manufacturing all need more wires.

Ultratech has launched Ultravolt with planned capex of ₹18 bn. Initial plant capacity has already started production ahead of schedule at Bharuch. The market compares this with the paint disruption. Lets look at numbers

Grasim's paint capex was ~65-70% of Asian Paint. Ultravolt's ₹18 bn capex is 30% of Polycab gross block. Plus, Polycab's gross block is expected to reach ~₹94 bn in FY28 while KEI could reach ~₹43 bn. Ultravolt's announced gross block is only ₹18 bn

The biggest advantage for Ultratech is raw material availability. Copper & Aluminium dominate industry economics and the Birla ecosystem already has deep expertise & inhouse production

Demand-intelligence advantage. Cement is purchased 6 months before wires in building construction. Ultratech can potentially spot demand trends 4-6 months ahead of competitors

Builder relationships, contractor network & Ultratech Building Solutions outlets create a ready-made ecosystem for cross-selling wires. That's a powerful advantage most new entrant

Ultravolt has prepared well. Better channel incentives, faster delivery commitments, aggressive marketing & strong retailer engagement are already creating buzz. But replicating the paint playbook won't be straightforward. 

Paints & cement share significant overlap in distribution. Wires are largely sold through electrical dealers, distributors, retailers & electrician networks. Building an electrical distribution franchise takes years

Another key difference is profitability. Leading W&C players operate at ~12-14% EBITDA margins, far lower than the 18-20%+ margins paint Co. enjoyed before disruption. With lower margins, room for aggressive pricing is limited

Further: Utility, industrial, railway, transmission & infra projects require extensive testing, approvals, certifications & execution history before meaningful scale can be achieved.
Conclusion: Birla has genuine advantage in raw material sourcing, builder relationships & demand visibility. But unlike paints, incumbents start with lower margins, stronger technical moats & entrenched distribution

Jury is still out. Ultravolt looks prepared. Space will remain interesting

Coforge Chairman resignation : Lets dig deeper

OP Bhatt's resignation came after disagreements around the Board evaluation process. In his resignation note, he says continuing on Board amid differences regarding his "good faith actions" would not be conducive to Board effective functioning 

OP Bhatt is not a conventional IT industry chairman. He is among India's most respected bankers, having led SBI between 2006-11 & later served on boards across large corporates including Tata Group companies

The market doesn’t take such update kindly, but Bhatt's continuation was already under question even before the resignation. Shareholders (inc largest shareholder Advent) voted against his reappointment as Independent Director from May'27
 
Let’s go a bit in history: The company was earlier known as NIIT Tech before its ownership transition & eventual rebranding to Coforge. Barings acquired control of NIIT in 2020, leading to ownership change then.

Later, Barings steadily monetised its stake through multiple block deals as the company scaled in size, profitability & market value. After Barings' complete exit by FY24, Co. become fully public market institutional owned.

OP Bhatt joined the board in 2024 & became Chairman during a phase when Coforge was pursuing aggressive scale-up ambitions. Coforge accelerated inorganic growth. The acquisition of Cigniti significantly expanded its engineering & digital capabilities under him.

The much bigger acquisition Encora was also under OP Bhatt. The acquisition materially increased Coforge's scale, global delivery footprint & exposure to high-growth digital engineering segments.

Encora also changed the shareholding landscape. Through the transaction, Advent became the largest shareholder in Coforge, making its views impossible for the board to ignore. That's why the key takeaway may not be the resignation itself. The bigger story could be that the largest shareholder & the Chairman were not aligned on important matters. 

The bullish view is that management execution remains intact. The cautious view is that whenever Chairman, Board & largest shareholder are not on the same page, governance questions emerge and mgmt. energy is focussed away from growth.

Impact of change in EV subsidy policy from 31 July 2026

PM E-DRIVE subsidy for electric 2Ws ended on 31 Jul 2026. Govt earlier plan was to support E2W till 31 Mar 2026, then gave the industry a 4-month extension till Jul-end as there was unutilized budget

PM E-DRIVE replaced FAME-II in Oct'24 with a 10,900 Cr outlay. The idea was simple: help EV adoption scale while supporting charging infra, buses, trucks & other EV segments

initially, e-2W buyers got subsidy of 5,000/kWh, capped at 10,000/ vehicle. That was a meaningful discount for mass-market scooters. From Apr'25, cut by half to 2,500/kWh with max capped at 5,000/Veh. Signalling gradual withdrawal of support.

Now for 2W, even that 5,000 support is gone. Effective acquisition cost of an EV scooter will move up. 5,000 price hike may not sound huge, but in entry-level its imp for price-sensitive consumer

Some moderation in electric 2W demand was expected. OEMs were preparing for it as subsidy-led growth gradually transitions to product-led growth. 

August EV 2W market share came lower than July. E2W MS has come down but not in 3w as July subsidy withdrawal only 2W not in 3W. August is typically a non-festival month & seasonality also matters. OEMs should absorb subsidy via better exchange / financing offers

Market is also looking for next phase of EV support. Discussions around "FAME III" continue, but indications suggest focus could shift towards vehicle other than 2W. 2W penetration already >10% while other segment need more support

If electric 2Ws are eventually excluded from future demand subsidies, industry economics will increasingly depend on product quality, distribution, service network & battery costs instead of govt incentives.

One factor often ignored: OEMs capacity are planned in a way where capacity expansion will happen in same facility. Hence, incremental capex intensity will be far lower. Gradual drivetrain shift will continue without large incremental capex

Bottom line: Subsidy withdrawal may create short-term demand noise, but the long-term story remains the same. India's 2W market is enormous, EV penetration is still low, and the migration from ICE to EV is likely to be a long, gradual journey rather than a subsidy-driven sprint.

**FCNR Sugar Rush What does it means for India**
FCNR experiment has turned into a blockbuster. Total inflows exceeded $136bn vs market expectations of ~$80bn. FCNR(B) deposits alone ~$127bn
  
Like Hindi movie, climax was amazing. 
Total inflows were ~$41bn by July-end, ~$73bn by Aug 21 and ~$136bn by Aug 31. Biggest forex mobilization drives India has ever seen. August was where the real frenzy happened. FCNR deposits jumped from ~$65.4bn on Aug 21 to ~$127.2bn by Aug 31.
  
Why did NRIs rush in? RBI effectively removed the pain point: currency hedging cost. Banks offered attractive yields while RBI absorbed swap costs For investors, FCNR became a rare risk-reward opportunity. Attractive $ returns + ability to leverage deposits (leverage run 4-5x)
  
FCNR nuance: Depositor takes bank credit risk but avoids INR depreciation risk since deposits remain in foreign currency. Currency mismatch is largely handled by RBI A key incentive for banks: incremental FCNR funds were exempted from CRR & SLR requirements.
  
More deployable money, less regulatory drag hence higher NIMs, Every $ mobilized can potentially earn better spreads for banks Flip side: Liquidity is now overflowing. System liquidity has surged sharply as these inflows entered the banking system

When banks are flush with money, appetite for wholesale funding drops. That's already showing up in lower CD rates & softer short-term funding costs Excess liquidity usually pushes overnight money market rates lower. Too much cash chasing too few opportunities compress yields
 
The RBI also gets a strategic advantage. Larger forex reserves and dollar balances improve its ability to manage forward market positions & reduce pressure from speculative USD demand. Forward dollar short should be reduced going forward
 
For currency speculator, the message is important. Betting aggressively against ₹ becomes tougher when RBI has significantly larger forex ammunition and stronger external buffers Now comes the hard part. Raising $136bn is the easy part.
  
Deploying it productively is the challenge. These are time-bound liabilities with an embedded cost. Eventually the money must earn more than it costs. INR already showing strength: USDINR below 95 today
 
The success of this scheme won't be judged by the $136bn raised. It will be judged by whether India converts this liquidity windfall into stronger growth, stable ₹, lower funding stress & productive credit creation over the next few years

The Relationship Trump Misunderstood:
For three decades, China and emerging markets effectively exported disinflation to the developed world. They produced goods at a fraction of Western costs and shipped them to consumers in the US and Europe. The result: lower prices and higher purchasing power
The West got cheaper TVs, phones, clothes, furniture and industrial goods. China got manufacturing jobs, export growth and rising incomes. It wasn't a one-way relationship. Both sides benefited
As exports surged, China accumulated enormous foreign exchange reserves. Every dollar earned from exports added to a growing pool of savings that had to be invested somewhere
Those reserves served two purposes: protect the yuan from volatility and build strategic national wealth. China used them to buy foreign assets, resources, companies and financial securities around the world
A large portion of those reserves found their way into US Treasuries. China became one of the largest lenders to the US government, recycling export earnings back into America's financial system
This mattered because sustained Treasury demand helped keep long-term US interest rates lower than they otherwise would have been. Cheap imports lowered inflation. Treasury purchases lowered financing costs
In effect, China was helping on two fronts: suppressing goods inflation through low-cost manufacturing and supporting bond markets through reserve recycling. 
Trump focused heavily on one side of the equation: the trade deficit. From that perspective, China was exporting too much and manufacturing jobs were leaving America. This became the basis for tariffs and trade confrontation.
But the other side received less attention. Those same imports were keeping prices low for US consumers. Many products became affordable precisely because they were manufactured in lower-cost economies
The relationship also extended to capital markets. China's reserve accumulation created a steady source of demand for US government bonds, helping support the broader financial system
Today that world is changing. China is no longer a low-income economy desperate for export growth. Wages have risen, technology has improved and its economic influence is far greater than it was 20 years ago
The old model of unlimited cheap labour, ever-rising globalization and automatic reserve recycling is fading. Both countries increasingly view the relationship through a strategic lens rather than purely an economic one
As supply chains fragment and tariffs rise, the US may face more inflation from its own policy choices. Producing goods domestically or through alternative supply chains is often more resilient, but rarely cheaper
At the same time, if foreign demand for Treasuries becomes less predictable, bond investors may demand higher yields to absorb increasing government debt. Higher yields mean higher financing costs across the economy
The next decade may look very different from the last three. Less globalization, more strategic competition, potentially higher inflation and structurally higher interest rates. Markets are still figuring out what that world looks like
Bottom line: The US-China relationship wasn't simply buyer vs seller. It was a system where goods, capital and inflation dynamics were deeply intertwined. Breaking that system may create consequences on both sides.
